content.text: Our modern world depends on energy. From powering our homes to fuelling our transport, we need reliable energy sources. Understanding the different energy resources—their advantages, disadvantages, and environmental impacts—is crucial for making informed decisions about our energy future.

Energy resources are classified as renewable (can be replenished within a human lifetime) or non-renewable (will eventually run out). The world is transitioning from non-renewable fossil fuels towards renewable alternatives.

rows.label: Will run out?
rows.left: No -- can be replenished naturally within a human lifetime
rows.right: Yes -- finite supplies that take millions of years to form

rows.label: Reliability
rows.left: Variable -- many depend on weather conditions (intermittent)
rows.right: Reliable -- can generate electricity on demand

rows.label: Energy density
rows.left: Low -- large areas needed for significant power output
rows.right: High -- small amounts of fuel produce large amounts of energy

rows.label: Location dependent
rows.left: Yes -- need specific geographic conditions (wind, sun, rivers)
rows.right: Less so -- power stations can be built in many locations

rows.label: Initial cost
rows.right: Variable -- nuclear is very expensive, gas plants are cheaper

rows.label: Running cost
rows.right: Variable -- ongoing fuel costs for fossil fuels

When comparing energy resources in exam questions, always discuss both advantages AND disadvantages. Consider reliability, environmental impact, cost, and whether the resource is renewable or non-renewable.
A coal power station burns 500 tonnes of coal per hour. The coal has an energy density of 24 MJ/kg. If the station is 40% efficient, what is its electrical power output?
Energy in coal per hour = 500,000 kg × 24 MJ/kg = 12,000,000 MJ = 12,000 GJ
Electrical output = 0.40 × 12,000 GJ = 4,800 GJ per hour
A wind turbine produces 2 MW when operating. If it operates at full capacity for 35% of the time (capacity factor), how much energy does it produce per year?
Effective hours at full capacity = 0.35 × 8760 = 3066 hours

Advantages: (1) No greenhouse gas emissions during operation, (2) Wind is a free and inexhaustible resource, (3) Low running costs once installed. Disadvantages: (1) Variable and unreliable output depending on wind conditions, (2) Visual impact on landscapes and noise pollution, (3) Can pose a risk to birds and bats.

Nuclear power is classified as non-renewable because it relies on uranium (or plutonium) as fuel, which is a finite mineral resource extracted from the Earth. Although nuclear fission produces no CO2 during electricity generation, the uranium fuel will eventually be exhausted and cannot be naturally replenished on a human timescale.
— Energy per day = 300 W x 4 h x 3600 s/h = 4,320,000 J. Energy per year = 4,320,000 x 365 = 1,576,800,000 J. Alternatively: 0.3 kW x 4 h x 365 days = 438 kWh per year. (calculation)

a) Gas power station: very reliable; can be turned on and off quickly to meet demand and operates independently of weather. b) Wind farm: unreliable; output depends on wind speed, which varies unpredictably, so cannot guarantee supply. c) Tidal power station: moderately reliable; tides are highly predictable and regular, but power output varies with the tidal cycle (not constant) and there are periods of low output between tides.

When biofuels are burned, they release CO2 into the atmosphere. However, the plants grown to produce biofuels absorb CO2 from the atmosphere during photosynthesis as they grow. If new plants are grown to replace those harvested, the CO2 absorbed roughly equals the CO2 released, making the net emission approximately zero over the full cycle.

a) Nuclear replacing coal: Advantages include zero CO2 emissions during operation and very reliable base-load power supply. Disadvantages include production of radioactive waste requiring long-term storage, high construction costs, long build times, and risk (however small) of accidents. b) Wind and solar replacing coal: Advantages include zero emissions during operation, no hazardous waste, and declining costs. Disadvantages include variable output requiring energy storage or backup generation, large land area requirements, and dependence on weather conditions.
